$comment: Who says which words in this chapter (docs/voice-narration-plan.md section 3). Drafted by `npm run voice:script`; a line with no entry is read by the narrator. A person checks each draft and sets `reviewed` to true; re-drafting only touches missing and stale entries.

lines.text: You stay at the singing hall instead of taking the shelf path. The yeti herder waits at the door with the kid goat under one arm. The kid is eating her scarf.
"My herd keeps stopping on the east ridge,"
"Ears up, all pointing one way. Something under the ice is ticking. I want to know what, before a goat finds it first. Will you help me look?"
The herder points at the east ridge.
"Soft snow up there. Haul the sled, or go light?"
Her sled has a coil of rope and a lantern tied on. The kid is chewing the rope.
You load the rope, the lantern and a bundle of hay. The kid climbs on the hay and will not get off.
"Hay is heavy when it has opinions."
You tie the lantern to your belt and loop the rope across your chest. The kid trots ahead.
"The crust only holds you if you do not stop."
The sled sinks to its runners. The kid sits on top like a queen.
The crust creaks under your boots. The kid bounces ahead, light as a snowflake.
At the top, the wind goes quiet. A line of goats stands on the ridge, ears pointed west, toward the hall. The kid joins them and points its ears too, very seriously.
The crust cracks, and you slide back. The kid bleats with laughter. The herder hauls you up by the rope.
On the ridge, a line of goats points their ears west, toward the hall.
The ridge is bare ice and wind. A dark hole the size of a bucket breathes out a cold, hooting draft.
Tick. Tick. Tick. On your pack, the Listening Chime leans on its cord, not at the hole, but up the glacier toward the oldest ice. Is the hole the answer?
You lie flat with an ear on the ice. It is very cold.
You lick a finger and hold it up. The wind changes its mind every few breaths.
You ring the chime over the hole. One clear note, not sour, no echo.
"I could have told you that. I didn't, but I could have."
The hole is only wind in a tube of ice.
The hole only hoots. The real ticking is west, toward the hall, and low, under the ice. You pack snow around the hole so no goat noses in.
The wind swings, and the hole hoots at you rudely. You lose the trail. Then the kid sits down right where the ticking is loudest: west, and low.
says the herder. You pack snow around the hole so no goat noses in.
West of the hole, three snow mounds lie in a row, and the ticking jumps between them. The kid dives into one and pops out of another.
Empty! The kid pops out three mounds away, already sliding.
A gust shoves the kid sideways. It slides on its belly toward thin ice over a melt pool. The herder is too heavy to follow.
she calls. The kid is having the best day of its life. How will you stop it?
You swing the loop. The kid sees it and thinks it is a game.
calls the herder. It is a game.
You take a breath for the low hall note. The kid's ears twitch.
You glide low over the melt pool. The kid sees you and squeals.
The kid pops into your arms and licks your chin with a very cold tongue.
She tucks her lunch bundle into your pack.
"For the climb. Do not tell the kid."
You miss. The kid slides into a soft drift and pops out with a snowy beard, very pleased.
the herder tells it. She tucks it in her coat, where it chews her buttons, and keeps her lunch bundle there too.
West of the ridge, the glacier splits in a long crack. Steam curls out, smelling like warm wet wool. The ticking comes from below. A narrow snow bridge crosses it.
"My herd goes the long way around,"
The snow bridge is thinner than a pancake in the middle.
The long way curves around deep shadows and old cracks.
Steam fogs your eyes as you fly.
On the far side, the herder counts heads.
Steam fogs everyone's eyebrows. The ticking is almost under your boots now.
The snow gives way. You slide onto a warm, steamy ledge below. The herder hauls you up, grunting.
The ticking is almost under your boots now.
Under a lip of ice stands an old yeti listening post: a pole topped with a carved ice cup, like a giant ear.
"She never found out what ticked. Put an ear in and tell me."
Here the ticking is louder, and it has a beat.
You hum the low hall note into the cup. The ice hums back, a little flat. The ticking answers a beat later. The herder's ears go up.
You count against your heartbeat. Tick, tick, pause, tick. It repeats. The kid counts too, with its hoof, wrongly and very confidently.
The herder joins your note, deep as a cellar.
You draw the ticks in the snow. The herder sets a claw beside each mark.
The pattern matches the song you learned in the hall: slow, slow, quick. The ticking is the hall note, answered from far below.
"Of course. Grandmother always said the hall had a cellar nobody could find."
The herder sets out a little stove of warm stones. The kid falls asleep on someone's boots.
"The tunnel below is too narrow for me,"
"I'll go around by the hall's back door and meet you."
She gives you a jar of glowing moss.
The tunnel mouth is a low arch of clear ice. Beyond it is dark. Your footsteps come back to you late, like a shy echo.
the herder calls after you. The ticking goes on ahead. How will you find your way?
The moss glows brighter near the ticks, as if it likes them.
"Is that a stitch or a feather?"
Hum, step, listen. The echo comes back from somewhere new each time.
The starlit frost glitters like a path of sugar.
The ticks run along the wall like stitches, then turn down to a crack at the tunnel's end.
someone whispers to the ticking. There, the tunnel shrinks around you. You will have to squeeze.
The frost blurs into feathers and more feathers. You bump the same wall twice.
someone mutters. The third time, you feel ticks under your hand. They lead to a crack where the tunnel shrinks.
The crack fits one body at a time, and no packs. Through it, the ticking is louder. Cold air slides out, smelling faintly of salt.
Part of the roof looks loose. How will you get through?
You chip with the rope hooks. Tink, tink, crunch.
a muffled voice calls through the ice. It is the herder, somewhere above.
Smallest first, then the packs, then the biggest.
someone asks. Everyone points at someone else.
The thornguard braces the roof like a table leg.
"This roof is heavier than it looks."
The duskrunner slides into the dark.
The crack is wide enough now. As you edge in, ice chips pat down from the roof. It gives a long, low creak.
The crack is only half as wide as you hoped. Ice chips rain on your heads, and the roof creaks.
someone says. Everyone gets frosty eyebrows.
The loose roof creaks, rests, and creaks again. Crawl only while it rests.

You come out in a small round chamber. One wall is smooth and warm: the back of the sealed seam, the crack in the singing hall's wall that hums when yetis sing. The ticking is loud as a heartbeat. The herder's voice comes faintly through the ice:
Pry the seam open quickly? Or answer its ticking and see what it does?
You hum the hall note softly at the seam, and wait. The seam ticks back, quicker. Frost sparkles down the wall in a pattern, over and over.
"It wants you to say it back,"
the herder calls through the ice.
"Grandmother said the ice talks, if you're polite."
The frost sparkles a pattern: tick, tock, tock, tick. The seam wants it said back.
the herder reminds you through the wall. Everyone sees the sparkles a little differently.
You slip through the corner crack into a narrow passage behind the singing hall. It smells of salt. Far off, the yetis in the hall hold their low note.
Ahead, the ticking stops, and something shimmers.

The passage ends at a fold in the air. Beyond its shimmer, you smell salt wind and hear gulls. The light around the fold is called Riftlight. Then your pack starts to hum. The Listening Chime is ringing all by itself, a thin note, answering the fold's low one. Nobody touched it.
someone whispers. What will you try?
You strike the chime. It was already humming, and now its note goes sour, with no echo.
In the quiet after, a lower note trembles under your feet.
Your starweaver studies the light. The others see only a shimmer.
someone asks. The opening hums back faintly. Nothing steps through, and nobody can name the place beyond.
You put an ear near the rock. Under the gull cries, a low note rises and falls.
Frost lines run toward the fold like the spokes of a wheel, and every line ticks. Beside it, someone long ago scratched a tally into the stone, one mark for each visit. There are not many marks.
Your taps and the ticking line up: slow, slow, quick. The fold brightens. A gull cries on the other side, very close.
The taps tumble into a clatter, and the fold dims. A puff of cold air ruffles your hair.
says somebody. You stop and listen instead: slow, slow, quick. It is the hall note, answered. The fold brightens again.
The herder squeezes in from the hall's wide back door, with hay in her fur and the kid under her arm. She sniffs the salt wind and steps back.
"My herd must never wander in there. Goats go through anything. How do we keep them out?"
You and the herder stack blocks across the passage mouth, leaving a gap for people. She tests each block with her shoulder.
You tie the herder's spare goat bells across the passage mouth. A goat that pushes through will ring like a party.
says the herder. The kid tries to eat a bell.
A bigfoot lifts the biggest blocks. Smash, thump, thump!
says the herder. The others fit small stones into the gaps.
Your bigfoot sets the last broad block, and everyone marks a gap for travelers.
"Not even the kid gets through that,"
says the herder. The kid looks offended.
The passage mouth is marked. Goats will stay out, and travelers will look before they step in. The herder pats the cairn like a friend's head.
"There. It can be as strange as it likes on the other side."
The herder finds a row of old tally marks scratched beside the fold.
"Maybe your song wakes it. Maybe it wakes what waits beyond. Your road, not mine."
She presses four coins from the hall's tin into your hand, and a small warm bead.
She eats it in two bites and looks embarrassed.
"The hay is not the only thing running low."
The kid gets the crust, and then eats her glove.
The herder scuffs the floor and frowns. Meltwater has left a slick skin of ice sloping toward the shimmer.
"One wobble, and somebody slides in feet first."
By the back door lie old planks and a little grit. The kid stares at a drip, fascinated.
You chip with your heels and the rope hooks.
You lay the planks and sprinkle grit on the thinnest ice.
A young yeti trots up with a sack of grit and a sign that says GRIT.
he says, in case you can't read. You spread it, and it bites into the ice. The kid eats a pinch and regrets it.
The floor grips your boots now. The herder stamps on it, then on the kid's tail by mistake, and everybody apologizes.
says the herder. Nobody will slide anywhere by accident.
A boot skids, and someone sits down hard. The thump makes the fold shiver.
the herder says, hauling them up, laughing. The floor is rough, but it holds.
The hall seam answered your song. Here the fold itself ticks to the beat of that song. The herder waits by the cairn, the kid asleep in her coat.
"Sing to it, and see what it does,"
"Or leave it sleeping, and come home. I won't think less of you."
Everyone takes a breath. The fold leans toward you, the way the seam did.
The note wobbles. Frost showers down every collar, sharp and cold. Then the herder hums the low part from the cairn, deep and slow.
You find your note. It is not tidy. It is enough.
You sing the low note. The ticking steadies. The fold widens, and salt wind brushes your cheeks. When you stop, it stays open.
You strike the chime once more. A clear note, and then an echo, coming back through the fold.
Beyond, shallow water ripples around mud. Cross together, or go back to camp first.
You stand together by the fold. The herder's cairn guards the passage mouth. She sniffs the salt wind.
"Things are moving that should stay put. What is moving them? Can anyone put them back?"
Your chime hums. For a moment it leans past the fold, up the glacier, toward the oldest ice.
The herder walks you back to the hall by the wide back door. Behind you the fold sleeps on, ticking.
"Who taught it? And why is the sea under my glacier?"
The Cairnstep lead is still yours, and you can come back to sing the note later.
The kid is so close you can hear it chewing.
You lose the beat, and your ear freezes to the cup. Ow! The herder breathes on it until it comes unstuck. Then she reads her grandmother's old marks on the pole.
"Like the hall song. Grandmother had it all along."
You jam the rope hooks into the seam and lean. The ice groans.
"Is it supposed to make that noise?"
Everyone takes a breath. The fold shivers away from the first sound, like a goat that has been grabbed once too often.
